assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-wavelength idea lets thousands of atoms be interrogated in a lattice free of motional and recoil shifts. It turned optical frequency standards into instruments at the 10^-18 level, with direct consequences for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic redshift measurements over millimetres and a future redefinition of the second. It is a clean, precisely understood piece of atomic physics where theory and experiment agree.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations. Ye's JILA group brought the strontium lattice clock to the highest accuracy and stability and tied it to the frequency comb. Two names are a natural and fair pairing; the supplied credit is compact. Some earlier ion-clock and comb work is already recognised (Hall and Hansch, 2005; Wineland, 2012).
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others) have built and compared lattice clocks, and the performance has been confirmed repeatedly. The field is mature and its impact is broad and still growing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier metrology prizes may weigh against it
Whether to include a third contributor, such as an early lattice-clock theory or ytterbium group, is not settled by the supplied credit
I have not independently checked the latest accuracy figures

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices became a controllable laboratory for many-body quantum physics: the superfluid-Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and, later, single-site microscopy. This is fundamental understanding of strongly correlated quantum matter, gained through the same atomic-physics toolbox I know well, and the impact reaches condensed-matter and quantum-information science.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) supplied the theory proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices; Greiner and Bloch carried out the decisive Mott transition experiment and developed it into a broad quantum-simulation platform. Esslinger's fermionic work is also important, so a four-person claim is real and the three-name selection is a hard choice. The Bose-Einstein condensation prize (2001) covers the underlying cooling but not this step.
assessment.maturity: The results are confirmed in many groups and have been extended for two decades. Recognition is timely, although quantum simulation of open problems such as the 2D Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram is still developing.
uncertainties: Credit allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger is unresolved
Some of the headline promises for solving open problems are not yet fulfilled
The theory and experiment contributions have a different time structure

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators revealed a new classification of electronic states based on topology and spin-orbit coupling, and the theory predicted robust edge or surface states that were seen experimentally. It is a deep, original conceptual advance with wide influence on materials science. I defer to my condensed-matter colleagues on the finer detail, but the discovery is clearly one that tells us something new about nature.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theoretical prediction and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Other contributors (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Hasan) have strong claims, so the three-name configuration leaves a real dispute. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions is related but separate.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent experimental confirmation exists in HgTe, Bi-based compounds and ARPES studies, and the interpretation is stable. The topic is mature and timely.
uncertainties: The attribution is contested among several theorists and experimentalists
Practical relevance remains limited, though it should not decide worthiness
My assessment of the condensed-matter details is less authoritative than that of colleagues in that field

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision (three-step) picture and the strong-field quantum theory of high-harmonic generation explain the harmonic plateau that was so unexpected and underpin all of attosecond science. The model is simple and physical: an electron is ripped off, driven by the field and brought back. It is the conceptual core of a field that is already recognised experimentally.
assessment.attribution: Corkum gave the semiclassical recollision picture, Lewenstein and co-workers the quantum theory, and Schafer and colleagues the early numerical and plateau-cutoff work. The three-name set is plausible, but Kulander and others have claims. I declare a close professional link to this field, so I weigh the attribution as carefully as I can.
assessment.maturity: The recollision model has been verified in many ways, including tomography and cut-off laws, and is now textbook. Because the 2023 prize already honoured the generation and measurement of attosecond pulses, the marginal value of a second prize in the area is a real question.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2023 attosecond prize
Open allocation of credit among Corkum, Lewenstein, Schafer, Kulander and others
My own closeness to attosecond physics and to some of those involved may bias me

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping and cooling antihydrogen and comparing its spectrum, and the proton and antiproton magnetic moments, with matter at parts per trillion or better tests CPT symmetry and the matter-antimatter asymmetry directly. The question is fundamental and the experiments are technically spectacular precision atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse's group did the trapped antiproton and positron work and made antihydrogen with ATRAP; Hangst led ALPHA, which trapped antihydrogen and measured its 1S-2S transition and charge neutrality; Ulmer's BASE measured the antiproton magnetic moment. The credit across ATRAP, ALPHA, ASACUSA and BASE is complex, and Gabrielse, Hangst and Ulmer capture much but not all of it.
assessment.maturity: Results from several collaborations agree with CPT invariance, but the measurements keep improving and no deviation has been seen. Recognition may be somewhat early as the programme is still evolving.
uncertainties: Negative result for CPT violation; the importance depends on the future precision
Credit is spread over several collaborations
Possible premature timing

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms provides a new way of measuring gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and it extends the wave nature of matter to heavy objects. It is a natural extension of laser cooling, with both fundamental physics and sensor applications.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group built the first atom interferometers with gratings, Bordé gave the theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, and Kasevich and Chu demonstrated light-pulse interferometers and precision gravimetry. Chu is already a laureate (1997) for cooling, and the proposed configuration omits Chu, so some contributions are not independent of earlier recognition.
assessment.maturity: The technique is firmly confirmed and has been used in many laboratories for g measurements and for fine-structure constant determinations. Maturity is high.
uncertainties: Interplay with the 1997 and 2001 prizes and with Chu and Ketterle
Allocation among the early grating and light-pulse groups
The fundamental-physics results to date are mostly confirmations

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Bringing mechanical oscillators of macroscopic size to their quantum ground state and entangling them with light or circuits speaks directly to where the boundary between quantum and classical lies. The ground-state cooling and quantum control experiments are clear and elegant.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis (not in the credited list) cooled a mechanical resonator to its ground state with a superconducting qubit; Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed cavity optomechanics, including sideband cooling and quantum-coherent coupling. The three-name set is defensible but leaves out other leaders of the field.
assessment.maturity: Ground-state cooling, squeezing and entanglement are reproduced by several groups. The field is still moving, and its larger foundational claims are not settled.
uncertainties: Compound field with several distinct achievements
Credit for the ground-state result is shared with people outside the supplied names
Foundational impact (macroscopic superposition) is not yet fully demonstrated

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire quantum materials, a tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons. It is original and has produced a very large body of work.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the 2018 experiments showing correlated states and superconductivity. The pairing of theory and experiment is natural, and the credit appears relatively clear, though other experimental groups also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Many laboratories confirmed the phenomena within a few years, but the origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated, so the interpretation is not yet stable. The recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved
Possible prematurity
I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on the relative importance
